title: India Is About to Launch a Producer Price Index for the First Time. It Will Replace a System the Country Has Used for Decades.
excerpt: The new PPI will track inflation in services — including banking, railways, and telecom — for the first time, bringing India in line with global statistical standards after two decades of debate.
body:
India is on the verge of one of its most significant economic data reforms in years. The government will launch a Producer Price Index (PPI) this month, replacing the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) that has been the country's primary gauge of producer-level inflation for decades. A new WPI series with an updated base year will also be released alongside it.

The shift has been discussed for over twenty years. The WPI, which tracks prices of goods at the wholesale level, has long been criticised for its narrow scope — it covers only goods and ignores services entirely. In an economy where services contribute more than half of GDP, that gap has grown harder to justify.

## What Changes

The PPI will include output prices, input costs, and — for the first time — a dedicated services component. The initial rollout will cover seven services: banking, securities transactions, insurance, pension fund management, railways, air passenger services, and telecom.

Praveen Mahto, the principal economic adviser at the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, confirmed that the new WPI series will use 2022-23 as the base year and will be released on June 15. The services PPI is expected to be published quarterly, in line with international practice.

## Why It Matters

The PPI tracks price movements before they reach consumers. By capturing what producers pay and charge, it provides an early signal of inflationary pressure — or relief — that the Consumer Price Index picks up only months later.

For policymakers at the Reserve Bank of India, this is a significant upgrade. The RBI currently relies on CPI for its inflation-targeting framework, but the absence of a robust producer-level index has left blind spots in how inflation transmission is understood. A PPI would help bridge that gap, enabling more precise and timely monetary policy decisions.

Over time, the PPI data will also be used to strip inflation from real growth calculations in the national accounts — a technical but important step toward making India's GDP figures more accurate and comparable internationally.

## The Diaspora Angle

For NRIs working in finance, economics, and data analytics, this is a milestone worth watching. India's statistical infrastructure has been a longstanding point of concern among international investors and rating agencies. The launch of a PPI, aligned with practices followed by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Eurostat, and other major economies, sends a signal that the government is serious about data credibility.

It also has practical implications. Better producer-level data will improve forecasting models used by everyone from commodity traders to multinational corporations with Indian supply chains. For the growing number of Indian-origin economists and analysts working in global institutions, the PPI will offer a richer dataset to work with.

## The Transition

The government plans a five-year transition from WPI to PPI, though officials have cautioned that the timeline will depend on how the new indices perform. The initial release will be closely watched — both for the quality of the data and for how it compares with existing WPI readings.

India's retail inflation stood at 3.48 per cent in April 2026, but the outlook is clouded by the Iran war's impact on energy prices and the forecast of the weakest monsoon in 11 years. The PPI will add a crucial new lens through which to track how those pressures flow through the economy — from producer to consumer, from factory gate to kitchen table.

Sources: Reuters, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), RBI
author: Diaspora Desk
